history.heading: Settlement and the Commonwealth
paragraphs: Iceland, a volcanic island just south of the Arctic Circle, was settled by Norse settlers from around 874, along with people from the British Isles, many of them enslaved. In 930 the settlers founded the Althing, one of the oldest parliaments in the world, at Þingvellir. Icelanders adopted Christianity around 1000 by decision of the Althing.
The Icelandic sagas, written in the 13th century, tell the stories of the settlers and are masterpieces of medieval literature. Leif Erikson, born in Iceland, reached North America around 1000.

history.heading: Norwegian and Danish rule
paragraphs: Iceland came under the Norwegian crown in 1262 and then under Denmark. Centuries of hardship followed, with a Danish trade monopoly, plague and volcanic eruptions; the 1783 Laki eruption caused a famine that killed about a fifth of the population.
A 19th-century independence movement, led by Jón Sigurðsson, gained home rule in 1904 and sovereignty in 1918 in union with Denmark.

history.heading: Republic
paragraphs: While Denmark was occupied in the Second World War, Britain and then the United States occupied Iceland. Iceland became a republic on 17 June 1944. It joined NATO in 1949 despite having no army.

Iceland fought the "Cod Wars" with Britain over fishing limits between the 1950s and 1970s, extending its zone to 200 nautical miles. Its banking system collapsed in the 2008 financial crisis. In 1980 Vigdís Finnbogadóttir became the world's first democratically elected female president.

culture.heading: Language and literature
paragraphs: Icelandic has changed so little that Icelanders can still read the medieval sagas. Most Icelanders use patronymic names (such as Jónsdóttir, "Jón's daughter") rather than family names. Iceland publishes more books per person than almost any country, and Halldór Laxness won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1955.
Musicians such as Björk, Sigur Rós and Of Monsters and Men have international followings.

culture.heading: Traditions
paragraphs: Most Icelanders belong to the Lutheran Church. Swimming pools fed by geothermal water are central to social life. Traditional foods include lamb, fish, skyr (a yogurt-like dairy product) and, at the midwinter festival Þorrablót, fermented shark. Iceland's men's football team reached the 2018 World Cup, the smallest country ever to do so.

politics.heading: Parliamentary republic
paragraphs: Iceland is a parliamentary republic. The prime minister leads the government, responsible to the Althing, while the directly elected president is head of state. Governments are usually coalitions. Iceland consistently ranks first in the world for gender equality.
Iceland is a NATO member without armed forces, relying on a defence agreement with the United States. It is not an EU member but is part of the European Economic Area and Schengen.

economy.heading: Fish, aluminium and tourism
paragraphs: Iceland has a high standard of living. Its economy rests on fishing, aluminium smelting, which uses cheap renewable energy, and tourism, which has boomed since the 2010s, attracted by glaciers, volcanoes, waterfalls and the Northern Lights.

Almost all electricity and heating comes from renewable geothermal and hydroelectric sources. The currency is the Icelandic króna. Volcanic eruptions on the Reykjanes Peninsula since 2021 have threatened the town of Grindavík.
